questions.prompt: The four 'cardinal' virtues -- so called because all other human virtues hinge on them -- are prudence, justice, fortitude, and:
choices: Temperance
Patience
Humility
Generosity
questions.explanation: 'Cardinal' comes from the Latin cardo, 'hinge.' These four virtues, acquired by human effort and habit, are the hinges on which a well-ordered moral life turns.
questions.hint: It's the virtue of self-moderation, keeping desires within due limits.

questions.prompt: 'Prudence,' as a cardinal virtue, means:
choices: Right practical judgment about what to actually do in a given situation
Timid caution that avoids all risk
Raw intelligence or high IQ
Following rules without thinking about them
questions.correctAnswer: Right practical judgment about what to actually do in a given situation
questions.explanation: Prudence isn't timidity -- it's the virtue that lets a person correctly discern the true good in a concrete situation and choose the right means to reach it.
questions.hint: It's about applying good judgment to a real decision, not just being smart in the abstract.

questions.prompt: True or False: 'Fortitude,' as a cardinal virtue, means feeling no fear at all.
questions.explanation: Fortitude is firmness in pursuing the good despite difficulty, danger, or fear -- not the absence of fear. It means acting rightly in spite of fear, not never feeling it.
questions.hint: A person can feel afraid and still have this virtue, as long as they act rightly anyway.

questions.prompt: The cardinal virtue of '____' ensures the will's mastery over instincts and keeps the desire for pleasures within due limits.
questions.explanation: Temperance doesn't mean suppressing every desire -- it means keeping legitimate desires (for food, drink, and other goods) rightly ordered rather than letting them run unchecked.
questions.hint: It's the same virtue named at the start of this topic's very first question.

questions.prompt: 'Justice,' as a cardinal virtue, is the constant and firm will to:
choices: Give God and neighbor their due
Win every argument
Punish wrongdoers as harshly as possible
Treat every situation identically, ignoring context
questions.correctAnswer: Give God and neighbor their due
questions.explanation: Justice orders our relationships toward the common good, respecting the rights of others and fulfilling our duties toward God and neighbor alike.
questions.hint: Think of 'giving each their due,' not 'winning' or 'punishing.'

questions.prompt: Match each cardinal virtue to its core meaning.

pairs.right: Right practical judgment about what to actually do
Giving God and neighbor their due
Firmness in pursuing the good despite difficulty or fear
Keeping desire for pleasures within due limits

questions.explanation: Together, the four cardinal virtues govern how we judge (prudence), relate to others (justice), face difficulty (fortitude), and handle desire (temperance) -- the hinges of a well-ordered moral life.
questions.hint: Each virtue answers a different question: how to judge, how to relate, how to endure, how to desire.

questions.prompt: Unlike the cardinal virtues, which are developed by human effort and habit, the theological virtues -- faith, hope, and charity -- are:
choices: Infused directly by God, disposing us to relate to him as our supernatural end
Earned entirely through years of ascetic discipline
Optional extras for especially devout Catholics
Available only to canonized saints
questions.correctAnswer: Infused directly by God, disposing us to relate to him as our supernatural end
questions.explanation: The theological virtues have God himself as their direct object -- they can't be acquired by repeated human acts alone, but are given by God, usually at Baptism, and adapt our faculties to share in his own life.
questions.hint: 'Theological' hints at the difference -- these are directly about God, not just about being a good person in general.

questions.prompt: True or False: Of the three theological virtues, St. Paul teaches that love (charity) is the greatest.
questions.explanation: Paul's hymn to love concludes: 'So faith, hope, love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.' Charity alone will remain in heaven, where faith gives way to sight and hope to possession.
questions.hint: This is from Paul's famous chapter on love, often read at weddings.

questions.prompt: ____ is the theological virtue by which we believe in God and everything he has revealed, because he is Truth itself and cannot deceive or be deceived.
questions.explanation: Faith is not a blind guess -- it's a reasonable trust grounded in who God is: Truth itself, who neither deceives nor can be deceived.
questions.hint: It's the first of the three theological virtues, usually listed before hope and charity.

questions.prompt: 'Hope,' as a theological virtue, is the virtue by which we:
choices: Desire and trust in eternal life and God's help to attain it
Merely wish for good luck in life
Assume everything will simply work out on its own
Avoid thinking seriously about the future
questions.correctAnswer: Desire and trust in eternal life and God's help to attain it
questions.explanation: Hope isn't wishful thinking or passive optimism -- it's an active trust that God will give the grace needed to reach the eternal life he promises, if we cooperate with him.
questions.hint: This virtue is directed specifically toward eternal life, relying on God's own help.

questions.prompt: True or False: 'Charity,' as a theological virtue, is essentially the same thing as ordinary human friendliness or being generally nice.
questions.explanation: Charity is the supernatural virtue of loving God above all things and neighbor as oneself for God's own sake -- something deeper than natural warmth, though it doesn't exclude it.
questions.hint: This virtue is specifically about loving God above all things, not just being pleasant to be around.

questions.prompt: Match each theological virtue to its object.

pairs.right: Believing God and everything he has revealed
Desiring and trusting in eternal life and God's help
Loving God above all and neighbor as oneself, for his sake

questions.explanation: All three theological virtues have God as their direct object -- what he has said (faith), what he promises (hope), and who he is, loved for his own sake (charity).
questions.hint: One is about believing, one about trusting the future, one about loving.

questions.prompt: The 'capital' or 'deadly' vices are called that not because each one is automatically a mortal sin, but because they:
choices: Give rise to other sins and vices, serving as their root or 'head'
Were the very first sins ever committed by anyone
All involve capital punishment under Church law
Can never be forgiven under any circumstances
questions.correctAnswer: Give rise to other sins and vices, serving as their root or 'head'
questions.explanation: 'Capital' comes from the Latin caput, 'head' -- these vices are the head or source from which many other sins branch out, not a special category immune to forgiveness.
questions.hint: Think of 'capital' as in 'head' or 'source,' the root Latin meaning -- not as in punishment.

questions.prompt: True or False: Pride is traditionally considered the first and most fundamental of the capital vices.
questions.explanation: Pride -- an excessive, disordered self-regard that refuses to acknowledge dependence on God -- is traditionally named first among the capital vices, often seen as the root from which the others grow.
questions.hint: This is the vice most directly opposed to humility before God.

questions.prompt: ____, the capital vice of resentment at another person's good fortune and secret pleasure at their misfortune, is directly opposed to the virtue of charity.
questions.explanation: Envy is sorrow at another's good, as though it diminished one's own -- the opposite of charity, which rejoices in the good of others as a friend would.
questions.hint: It's the vice at work when someone else's success feels like your loss.

questions.prompt: 'Sloth' (acedia), as a capital vice, is best understood as:
choices: A spiritual apathy or sluggishness that resists the effort love of God requires
Simply being physically tired at the end of a long day
Taking a legitimate day of rest
Enjoying leisure time with family or friends
questions.correctAnswer: A spiritual apathy or sluggishness that resists the effort love of God requires
questions.explanation: Sloth isn't ordinary tiredness or healthy rest -- it's a spiritual sluggishness so deep it refuses the joy that comes from God, neglecting the effort love of him actually requires.
questions.hint: This is about the soul's laziness toward God, not the body's need for sleep.

questions.prompt: True or False: 'Gluttony' refers only to eating too much food, and has nothing to do with drink or other bodily pleasures.
questions.explanation: Gluttony traditionally names a broader disordered attachment to food and drink -- excess, but also excessive fussiness, eating too eagerly, or too often -- not just overeating narrowly defined.
questions.hint: This vice is opposed to the same virtue that governs desire for pleasure more broadly.

questions.prompt: Match each capital vice to the virtue it most directly opposes.
questions.explanation: Each capital vice is a distortion or refusal of a corresponding virtue -- growth in virtue is, in large part, the slow uprooting of these very tendencies.
questions.hint: Each vice is essentially the absence or corruption of one specific virtue.

questions.prompt: Isaiah 11 lists seven gifts of the Holy Spirit that rest upon the Messiah and, through him, upon believers. Which of these is one of the seven?
choices: Wisdom
Patience
Kindness
Self-control
questions.explanation: The seven gifts are wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord. Patience, kindness, and self-control are instead traditionally counted among the fruits of the Spirit, not the gifts.
questions.hint: The other three options are actually fruits of the Spirit, not gifts -- a different, though related, list.

questions.prompt: True or False: The 'fruits of the Spirit,' as listed by St. Paul in Galatians, include love, joy, peace, and patience.
questions.explanation: Paul's list in Galatians 5:22-23 begins: 'love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control' -- visible signs that the Spirit is truly at work in a life.
questions.hint: This list comes from Paul's letter to the Galatians, right after his list of the 'works of the flesh.'

questions.prompt: The Catechism describes the fruits of the Spirit as the first ____ of eternal glory -- perfections formed in us as the Spirit's work begins to bear visible results.
questions.explanation: The image is agricultural: just as a tree's fruit shows the tree is healthy, the Spirit's fruits in a soul are the first, visible signs of the glory that awaits in full at the end.
questions.hint: It's the same word already used earlier in the sentence, describing what these perfections are called.

questions.prompt: The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord) exist to:
choices: Complete and perfect the virtues of those who receive them
Replace the need for faith, hope, and charity entirely
Benefit only priests and consecrated religious
Apply only to the twelve apostles historically
questions.correctAnswer: Complete and perfect the virtues of those who receive them
questions.explanation: The gifts don't compete with the virtues -- they make a person docile to the Holy Spirit's promptings, perfecting the virtues so a person can respond readily to God's inspiration.
questions.hint: Think of these gifts as fine-tuning the virtues already present, not replacing them.

questions.prompt: True or False: 'Fear of the Lord,' as one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, means being terrified of God as a harsh, arbitrary judge.
questions.explanation: This gift means filial reverence and awe before God's holiness and goodness -- the fitting response of a child toward a father worthy of total respect -- not the servile terror of someone facing an unpredictable tyrant.
questions.hint: Think of a child's reverent respect for a good father, not dread of a threatening stranger.

questions.prompt: Match each list to where it comes from and how it's acquired.

pairs.left: Seven gifts of the Holy Spirit

pairs.right: Developed through human effort and habit

questions.explanation: These four lists work together in the spiritual life: virtues form good habits, gifts make us docile to the Spirit, and fruits are the visible evidence the Spirit is truly at work.
questions.hint: Two of these pairs point to a Scripture source; two point to how the virtues are acquired.

questions.prompt: The Beatitudes, which open the Sermon on the Mount, describe:
choices: The perfection of virtue that leads to true blessedness
A list of Old Testament ceremonial laws
A prayer recited only during the Easter Vigil
The formal requirements for becoming a bishop
questions.correctAnswer: The perfection of virtue that leads to true blessedness
questions.explanation: The Beatitudes depict the heights of the virtuous life, portraying the paradoxical road -- poverty of spirit, mourning, meekness, hunger for righteousness -- that leads to genuine, lasting blessedness.
questions.hint: This is Jesus' own portrait of what a fully virtuous, blessed life looks like.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Beatitude 'Blessed are the poor in spirit' is only about material poverty, and has nothing to do with a person's inner disposition.
questions.explanation: 'Poor in spirit' is traditionally read as spiritual humility and detachment -- a heart not clinging to riches or self-sufficiency -- though it doesn't exclude or dismiss the situation of the materially poor either.
questions.hint: The phrase specifies 'in spirit,' pointing to an inner disposition, not just a bank balance.

questions.prompt: 'Blessed are the ____ in heart, for they shall see God' -- the Beatitude traditionally connected to a purified, undivided love of God above all things.
questions.explanation: A heart wholly, simply directed toward God -- undivided by disordered attachments -- is what fits a person to see God as he is.
questions.hint: It's the opposite of a heart divided between God and other loves.

questions.prompt: The Beatitudes ultimately describe:
choices: The face of Christ himself, and the path of discipleship that conforms us to him
An impossible standard no one is actually meant to follow
Rules that apply only to clergy and religious
A poem with no real moral content
questions.correctAnswer: The face of Christ himself, and the path of discipleship that conforms us to him
questions.explanation: The Beatitudes aren't an abstract checklist -- they portray Christ's own character, and the Christian life is the slow work of being conformed to that same portrait.
questions.hint: The one who preached the Beatitudes also lived every one of them perfectly himself.

questions.prompt: True or False: Blessedness (beatitudo), in Catholic moral theology, is essentially the same thing as fleeting worldly pleasure or comfort.
questions.explanation: Blessedness is a deeper, lasting happiness found in union with God -- so real that the Beatitudes can call the poor, the mourning, and the persecuted 'blessed,' states that offer little worldly pleasure at all.
questions.hint: Notice who Jesus calls 'blessed' -- mourners and the persecuted are not exactly comfortable.

questions.prompt: Match each Beatitude to what it promises.

pairs.right: Theirs is the kingdom of heaven

questions.explanation: Each Beatitude pairs a state that looks like loss by worldly standards with a promise only God can fulfill -- the reversal at the heart of the Gospel.
questions.hint: Each promise directly answers the specific condition named just before it.
